record.paper_title: Open problems on graphs arising from geometric topology
record.original_question: Find combinatorial conditions that recognize when a colored graph represents a homology n-sphere for n >= 3.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
An (n+1)-colored graph is a pair (G, c) where G is a finite multigraph that is regular of degree n+1 (loops not allowed) and c : E(G) → {0,1,…,n} is an edge coloring such that any two edges sharing a vertex receive distinct colors. To such a graph one associates an n-dimensional simplicial pseudocomplex K(G) as follows: take one n-simplex σ_v for each vertex v of G, label the n+1 vertices of σ_v by the colors 0,1,…,n, and whenever two vertices u,v of G are joined by an edge of color i, glue σ_u and σ_v along their (n−1)-faces opposite to the vertex labeled i, matching vertex labels. For i ∈ {0,…,n}, let G_î denote the subgraph of G whose edges are those whose color is different from i. The graph (G, c) is said to represent (or to be a "gem"/crystallization of) a closed PL n-manifold M when K(G) is PL-homeomorphic to M; equivalently, every connected component of G_î (for each i) represents the standard PL (n−1)-sphere.

Problem. For each integer n ≥ 3, give a set of purely combinatorial conditions on an (n+1)-colored graph (G, c), checkable directly from G and c (for example in terms of the bipartite/connectivity structure of its bicolored subgraphs G_{ij} and their numbers of components, or other intrinsic invariants of (G, c)), that are necessary and sufficient for K(G) to be a homology n-sphere, i.e. for K(G) to be a closed PL n-manifold with the same integral homology groups as the n-sphere S^n.
artifact.status_search_result: No combinatorial characterization of colored graphs representing homology n-spheres for n ≥ 3 appears in the literature. Sphere recognition is known to be undecidable for n ≥ 5 and no polynomial-time algorithm is known in dimensions 3 and 4, so even algorithmic recognition is generally hard. The problem remains an open research direction in the crystallization theory of PL manifolds.

status_evidence.title: Frontiers of sphere recognition in practice
status_evidence.snippet: sphere recognition is known to be undecidable in dimensions five and beyond, and no polynomial time method is known in dimensions three and four
status_evidence.claim: General sphere recognition is undecidable in high dimensions and computationally hard in low dimensions, suggesting that purely combinatorial recognition of homology spheres via colored graphs is not known.

status_evidence.title: Manifold crystallization - Encyclopedia of Mathematics
status_evidence.snippet: An (n+1)-coloured graph encodes a closed PL n-manifold iff its bicolored subgraphs represent standard PL spheres.
status_evidence.claim: Standard background defining when colored graphs represent PL manifolds; no analogous characterization for homology spheres is recorded.
